utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: You don't recall that this convoy went through the corn fields under the escort of the ZNG members from Bogdanovci and that's how it reached the Vukovar hospital? It did not actually follow the agreed-upon route and what you are describing actually happened only on the way back.

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Had these been members of the ZNG, it would not have gone to the Vukovar barracks because once it entered the area of Vukovar, it spent the first night at the Vukovar barracks, which was under the control of the JNA. So it's not logical that ZNG members would have brought the convoy to the Vukovar barracks where the JNA were.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Then we are not talking about the same convoy. I realise that now that you mention the Vukovar barracks. However, when we are talking about this convoy that you are talking about now that reached the Vukovar barracks, do you know the reason why it didn't continue to the Vukovar Hospital? Was that because the Vukovar defence command did not want to let the convoy through in order not to disrupt the defence lines?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is partially true, because specifically Branko Borkovic got angry because this route was agreed upon, because it would have allegedly disrupted their lines of defence. However, in the Vukovar events, that was not the only reason, because the other parts were controlled by one side or by the other side. It was very important to the Croatian side to bring out the convoy with the wounded because the Croatian public was convinced that these large number of wounded were in danger. So the Vukovar defence was ordered to act even at its own harm in order to pull out the wounded. So that's what was done. I cannot, however, tell you how the JNA acted because I was not able to see that from the place where I was. However, it did take the convoy five days to go and come back.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: A little bit earlier, I talked about a different convoy, the convoy of the 18th of October, 1991, which was organised under the auspices of Medecins Sans Frontieres and which was brought to the Vukovar Hospital with the escort of members of the ZNG and on which occasion 111 sick and wounded persons -- 112 sick and wounded persons were evacuated. This is the convoy that I was talking about. Perhaps it was a misunderstanding.

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. That is the same convoy. The Medecins Sans Frontieres organised only one convoy, and that was the first convoy to bring out the sick and wounded from the Vukovar Hospital. I don't know when the second convoy took place. It's written down somewhere. But that convoy, which came out on the 18th of October, was actually that first convoy that we are talking about, based on an agreement with the JNA on the 8th of October. So it was immediately embarked on to organise this convoy.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: There is testimony about this convoy by people from the Doctors Without Borders or who were with them. So I won't ask you any more about that because it doesn't seem that you know so much about these two convoys.

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These people who wanted to do that at the time, I think had they been able to do that, they really deserve to be decorated, but I really believe that at that time they were not able to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Do you know how long the road between Vukovar and Vinkovci was open? How long did the traffic proceed normally?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The traffic did not proceed in a normal manner for a long time. As far as I can remember, and according to the information that I have, all exits and entrance points to Vukovar were closed on the 1st of October up to Marinci. This corresponds to what I have, because on the 30th of September, I spent all night in the defence command at Bogdanovci attempting to get in. There was a lot of shelling. Marinci fell the next day. And that's when all the access points to Vukovar were closed. At least this applied to the Croat side. We were at Marinci and that's how it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: I think that in responding to my question, you took out some kind of note or document. Could you please tell us what that is?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the sad occasion of the fall of Vukovar, on the 18th of October [as interpreted], the Vecernji List, Croatian Daily, published an overview of the events at Vukovar and that's where they described the day when Marinci fell. I had forgotten that. So that is why I used this document in order to see exactly the date whether Marinci fell.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: And when was this newspaper published?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was published this year. It was published several years -- several days ago, just prior to the anniversary of the fall of Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Just one intervention for the transcript. In the transcript it states that you said that Vukovar fell on the 18th of October, but you actually meant the 18th of November?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I meant the 18th of November.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: During the time shortly before the fall of Vukovar, were negotiations conducted with the JNA for an exchange of prisoners and were the prisoners from Vukovar mentioned on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were negotiations with the JNA about prisoner exchange, and that -- those negotiations were conducted by Mr. Ivan Milas on the Croatian side, by Andrija Raseta from the JNA. I don't remember whether anybody was assisting him or not, but I think there were two colonels from the security administration who were with him all the time and they were assisting him. That agreement, as far as I can recall, was signed on the 6th of November, 1991 under the principle all-for-all.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: In the implementation of that agreement, was a group of KOG members exchanged for Dr. Bosanac and Dr. Njavro, the ones who had been arrested in Zagreb for creating the Labrador association, network?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That group was exchanged with a number of important detainees, in the sense that the public was aware of them. I don't know whether Drs. Bosanac and Njavro were a part of that group. I wasn't really following the events.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: You told us that these were people who were important, as far as Croatia was concerned. Was this decision then made at the highest political level, to exchange these people?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It probably was.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: What about these persons who belonged to the Labrador group? Were they important too?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Not to Croatia. Not even their names were known, unlike the other group. However, obviously the negotiators had agreed on this being a fair deal and that's why the agreement was eventually reached.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Do you know what crimes these members of the Labrador group were accused of?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Illegal enemy activity, something like that, but I don't remember specifically, terrorism, sabotage, because certain specific particular acts were attributed to them in the Croatian territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: What about Mr. Aleksandar Vasiljevic? Was he involved with this exchange?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: After the arrest of the Labrador members, was the entire network in the police and general political environment in the Republic of Croatia uncovered?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not a member of the security services of the Republic of Croatia at the time. When I became adviser for national security, I didn't ask any questions about this case. It was no longer interesting. However, I did read the Belgrade newspaper, Duga, and I realised that some individuals had been tried in Belgrade. It transpired that documents had been left behind about a network of associates throughout the former Yugoslavia. These documents were being held by that detachment.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: We are talking about the network of associates that we discussed a while ago. They were the reason that the 2nd Detachment was given the task of contacting members of the Croatian MUP and some members of the Croatian media; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Did this group have anything to do with the incident at the Jewish cemetery in Zagreb?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The conviction prevails in Croatia, among the people, this has not been proved at trial. I know that proceedings were at one point underway, that it was this body that carried out the act of sabotage at the Jewish cemetery, by laying explosives to a monument in the Jewish cemetery as well as the Jewish community building in Palmoticeva Street in Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: As a former security officer, can you tell us this: How important is it for a security operation to keep its network of associates unknown?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is absolutely material. Each and every member of the service has a sacrosanct duty to keep it secret.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Were a network to be blown, it would be very difficult to very quickly organise another network in the same area, would it not?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Trust is lost, confidence is lost in the service, and these are some of the guidelines here in their work.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Is this a convenient time, then, Mr. Vasic?

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We will resume at 10 minutes to 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Vasic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: General, did you know that during the talks between the Croatian leaders and the representatives of the European Community regarding the recognition of Croatia, there was talk of the crime committed by the Croatian forces in Gospic back in 1991?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which talks do you have in mind? Where and when were these talks held?

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: What I meant was is this a problem in a very general sense? Are you familiar with the crimes committed in Gospic?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure if that point was raised. I was never party to any of these talks. Although from time to time, in our talks, Raseta mentioned the fact that there had been harassment and even murder. However, I was not myself specifically aware of any such incidents at the time. I knew nothing about Gospic at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: What about now?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know because the Croatian General Mirko Norac was tried and Tihomir Oreskovic was tried. I know that crimes were committed in the area and they were duly sentenced.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Do you know anything about an organised group named Opera?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I learned about this group later on. I learned from the media, from the printed media, and especially from articles published in the Belgrade newspaper Duga. This was serialised.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: What was the objective of that group?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe I learned this from one of Vasiljevic's interviews. I don't remember it all too clearly, though. However, based on my understanding, what my understanding was at the time, as I was learning about it, because I was familiar with certain people who were involved, I understood the objective was to collect funds, and these funds were later manipulated, which is what they were accused of. Supposedly they had been collecting funds in order to pay for psychological warfare throughout the different wars in the former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Do you know if they issued announcements or leaked information and thereby participated in psychological warfare in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was psychological warfare at work in Croatia at the time and propaganda, up until the end of the war in 1995. It is still at work, as a matter of fact. Who was involved and who payrolled the entire thing is not something that I can say. I was not involved on the Croatian side and certainly not on the other side.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Let's go back now to an earlier period, when you first joined the National Guards Corps and became Chief of Staff. Do you know anything about the activities of Mr. Tomislav Mercep with regard to the setting up of the National Guards Corps?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm aware of some of Tomislav Mercep's activities but nothing to do with the setting up of the National Guards Corps. He was not involved in that. The corps is a different organisation. Its leadership was in Zagreb. As far as I know, and I think I'm right on this one, Tomislav Mercep was not involved. Tomislav Mercep was Defence secretary for Vukovar municipality and he was involved in organising Vukovar's defence system and in the general area too.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: What about Vukovar's defence units organised by Mr. Mercep, as you say? Were those a part of the ZNG too?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. They were not part of the ZNG. At the time, before the fall of Vukovar, ZNG had set up four brigades. Those were not fully manned, nor did they have sufficient weapons. As for Vukovar's defence, on the inside, there was a relatively small number of people involved who were formally speaking members of the ZNG. All the other people that he organised were volunteers bringing their own weapons which they obtained in some way or purchased but they were not formally speaking members of the ZNG, except for a very small number of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: So these units organised by Mr. Mercep were paramilitary units, if I understand you correctly, made up of volunteers who just obtained weapons in one way or another?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Formally speaking, I can't agree that these were paramilitary units. Those were units, individuals, or groups, organised in part along military and police lines, along territorial lines. They prepared to defend Vukovar and they eventually defended Vukovar. The secretary for All People's Defence was Tomislav Mercep. How he went about doing this is a different matter altogether, but what I'm telling you is how it was in a formal sense.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Formally speaking, I don't think that the setting up of any such units had any basis in the existing laws of the SFRY or Croatia for that matter, or the constitution. I hope we can agree on this.

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To a certain extent I can agree that, formally speaking, this was the case. However, the situation on the ground showed a different reality. Early in 1991, the Serbian League was established. In April 1991, the Serbian League or Serbian Association proclaimed its annexation to Serbia. What was the All People's Defence secretary on the ground doing? He was preventing things like these from happening. He was helping to prevent some of these illegal activities.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Do you know that Mr. Mercep organised units comprising more than 1.000 men? Do you know that he reviewed these units in March 1991 in Bogdanovci?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't believe that over 1.000 people were involved. It would have been a very good thing for the defence once there was combat, once there was fighting. I know that he hailed from Bogdanovci and that his popularity was the greatest in Bogdanovci. He had a lot of his own men there. If he reviewed any units or not is not something that I can say. I simply don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: You refer to the Serb National Council, a league, and its decisions. Do you know that following the first multi-party elections in Croatia, where the HDZ won, on the 22nd of December, 1991 the Croatian constitution was changed and the Serbian people, who had up to that point been a constituent people in the Republic of Croatia became a national minority?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that the constitution was passed at that time. I know that the Serbian people used to be a constituent people but were then reduced to a lesser status. The republican leaders, however, were entitled to pass a new constitution and this was an assessment that they made at the time. Serb delegates who were ethnic Serbs, although many of them were not elected as members of Serb parties but, rather, other parties, had the duty to fight in the parliament to keep these changes from coming into effect.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Do you perhaps know that the Cyrillic script ceased to be used for official documents in the Republic of Croatia and the Cyrillic script, as we know, is used by most Serbs?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know if there was an official ban, but I do know that in the Republic of Croatia, among the Serbs residing in the Republic of Croatia up to 1990, the Cyrillic script was not used very much. I knew the script, although it's not one that I use in my mother tongue. Even the Serbs in Belgrade didn't use it all that much. I have relatives there, so I should know.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: We were both taught both these scripts, and we are familiar with both. But if you look at the political aspect of this problem, well, that's a different thing. If you introduce a ban on a script that a certain group is using, justifying this with the fact that only a minority appear to be using that script, well, that's a different thing, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree that there should be no bans at all and everybody should be allowed to use whatever script they prefer. However, if an official decision was made and adopted by official bodies of the Croatian government, I would consider that to be uncivilised.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: In this situation, on the eve of the multi-party elections, did representatives of the Serbian people had a national party such as the HDZ was for the Croats? Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe they did have a party, because there were literally dozens of parties in Croatia at the time. The HDZ was the most popular, and it won. I do know, however, that there were a lot of Serb representatives who were elected who were members of the SKH. I think that was the name, the party for democratic change.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: This party was headed by Ivica Racan an ethnic Croat, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: And this party continued to work along a communist line, modified for the purposes of this new period in history, but it had its roots in the communist era, didn't it?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm a soldier and I wouldn't go too far into these matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You said a while ago that you knew some things about the activities of Tomislav Mercep. Do you know about his activities in Vukovar itself in June or July 1991, August, all the way up until September 1991?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I became the Chief of Staff of the ZNG on the 10th of August 1991, and that's when I began to inform myself about the situation and the state of the defence in the territory of Croatia. Vukovar was already topical at that time. There were problems relating to the organisation. Many delegates, quote/unquote, and many people from Vukovar originally who actually lived in Zagreb would come to see me, asking for help. They also suggested solutions. They asked for help in equipment or in organisational matters. On those occasions, I found out that Tomislav Mercep, somebody I had only heard about at the time, whom I didn't know very well, was at the head of the organisation as the secretary of defence and that essentially is his duty to organise the defence. I heard that he was incompetent, that he had made some quite intactful moves, that he was alienating and picking fights amongst the people, not only amongst the Serbs but also amongst his associates, and there were requests that he be replaced. This is not something that I had only heard about. This had reached the top leadership as well because he was one of the leading people within the ruling party. Sometime in late August, perhaps around the 20th of August, or perhaps a bit later than that, he was replaced from that post by the president of the republic, and after some time he was brought to Zagreb in order to shed light on his activities in the area of Vukovar. There was an investigation by the ministry for internal affairs, and this is documented. At the time, I didn't actually have time for that. Later, I wasn't really interested in finding out exactly what it was that he did and what did the records indicate, what were his failings, what were his good and bad qualities.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: You said that you received information about bad defence organisation. Did any information about crimes committed by members of Mercep's forces in the area of Vukovar reach you committed around July 1991?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't know about reports that such-and-such a person was abused, expelled and so on, but I did learn about him detaining certain people. However, this did not refer only to Serbs, although it did refer mostly to Serbs. It was mostly about those who did not share his views. Exactly who these people were, I believe that there are records of that in documents of the Ministry of Internal Affairs of Croatia. I don't know if there are records about it also in the security services of the Croatian army because at the time I was not there at the head of the service.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: You said that when you were the head of the security service of the ZNG, you said at the time that the ZNG had four brigades. This number of brigades, part of which was -- which was part of the Croatian army, did it grow to 21 in due course?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The ZNG had four brigades. Later, as years went by, the 7th and the 9th were still formed. So two more. So the ZNG thus had six brigades. However, brigades were formed as part of the Croatian army. Because of tradition they continued to be known as the ZNG Brigades, the 1st, 2nd, 3rd and 4th, and then after that the 5th, 7th and the 9th. Excuse me, there were actually seven, in fact. They bore that name. But the rest which was mobilised by the army went to the -- to form brigades of the Croatian army. I don't know exactly what the numbers are. That's perhaps not so important. By the end of the war, or by the end of 1991, about 60 such brigades were formed. I don't know whether it was 21 until October. I'm not sure about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: In your statement, as well as in your evidence in another case before this Tribunal, you said that 24 brigades were formed until the 1st of October 1991, half were armed and by the end there were 63 in all and that they were all armed with weapons returned by the JNA.

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell us which units of the Croatian army operated in the area of Vinkovci, Vukovar, in 1991?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was the defence of Vukovar within Vukovar, which did not have any numerical insignia and it did not have any kind of military status, in terms of being a platoon, a company, a battalion, brigade and so on. This was later regulated through orders, and there are still disputes about exactly which brigade it was and whether it was a brigade at all. So the defence of Vukovar formed one entity. On the eastern front, there were units which had an effect on the defence of Vukovar or were preventing the advances of the JNA from the eastern front, and these were the 106th Brigade, 107th Brigade, then there was the 3rd ZNG Brigade, the 105th Brigade was there, a part of the 108th Brigade, and the 123rd Brigade. I might have left one out, and if I have, then I don't think it's all that important.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Can you please tell me whether the units that you mentioned also include the units that were in the area between Vukovar and Osijek? Are those units included?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The area between Vukovar and Osijek had relatively few units. For example, the 101st Brigade was there from Vukovar to Osijek, somewhere on the Vuka River or in the village of Vuka. The 122nd Djakovo Brigade was there. Specifically, the Djakovo Brigade. Osijek, Vukovar, was an area that had been occupied a while back, and there was only this line that remained which I drew, which went south of Vukovar, encircled some villages and then there were these brigades that I mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell us approximately what the strength of all of these brigades was? You don't have to give us a specific number.

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The brigades were mobilised, equipped, if the equipment was available, and were sent to the front. That was the situation. So in the beginning, in October, in September, there were relatively few units there. After the 10th, as the mobilisation proceeded, there were more. When Vukovar was occupied and when the front stabilised in that area, I believe that there were not more than 30.000 soldiers on the Croatian side, but this is hard for me to say specifically. This is just an estimate. A brigade numbered 2.000 soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Excuse me, for the transcript, earlier you said in October. In the transcript it states the 10th. So when you say -- said the 10th, actually, did you mean the day the 10th, as a date, or did you mean the tenth month, October? Earlier we already spoke about the decision of the chief of the General Staff, about the withdrawal of weapons belonging to the republics and the autonomous provinces. Do you know how the ZNG armed itself? And what was the time period in which the arms arrived? What did you know about this when you were a JNA officer and then later when you joined the ZNG?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the ZNG was formed on the 28th of May, 1991. There was a well-known review on the football grounds of the Zagreb football club. That's where the units were reviewed. From 1991, it armed itself with weapons obtained previously by the Ministry of Defence of the Republic of Croatia and the Ministry of Internal Affairs of the Republic of Croatia. And as far as I know, this is something that was written and talked about in the JNA, throughout Yugoslavia and in Croatia. These were Kalashnikovs which were purchased from what I know -- the numbers we are talking about are approximately 40.000 Kalashnikovs and some pistols. These are all the weapons that the ZNG were able to use or had at their disposal at the time they were formed, not all of these 40.000 pieces, because units of the MUP also received a certain quantity and a certain quantity had already been distributed. So when the ZNG was formed, they were -- there was the option to arm with the Kalashnikovs about 8.000 members.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Does that mean that the priority in using these weapons was given to the Ministry of Internal Affairs and then what was left over was given to the ZNG?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That is correct. But the ZNG was also part of the Ministry of Internal Affairs. All members of the ZNG signed their contracts with the minister of the internal affairs and carried out their duties within the ZNG as part of the MUP, because MUP was permitted to organise an armed unit, whereas the Ministry of Defence was not authorised to do something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Are you asserting that members of the ZNG were actually members of regular police forces?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Members of the ZNG were essentially formed out of the so-called reserve forces of the Ministry of Internal Affairs.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: This quantity of weapons that you mentioned, these 40.000 Kalashnikovs, long-barrelled weapons, is that the quantity of weapons obtained by General Spegelj? This is something that was made public in the former Yugoslavia, I think, in January 1991.

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I think that that is probably the shipment of arms obtained by General Spegelj. I don't know whether anyone else obtained these arms, but this refers to that famous footage of the arms shipment organised through General Spegelj.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Was blocking the barracks also another source of weapons for the ZNG?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That is correct. That was an additional source to obtain weapons for the ZNG, which actually turned into the main source, and that source made it possible to end the war in Croatia in the way that it ended. Because on the 1st of September 1991, the international community declared an embargo on arms shipments for the entire territory of the former Yugoslavia. Croatia had no other sources. It was under threat. And it had to organise itself and obtain weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Were 230 tanks taken in this way from the Varazdin barracks?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that it was not actually that number. I think it's about 130 tanks but you probably have the record with the numbers from the JNA. But I believe that it's about 100-odd armoured vehicles, tanks, armed personnel carriers and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: One of the strongest armoured corps was located in Varazdin?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we didn't call it an armoured corps. These were just corps of the infantry corps, but they did have a lot of armoured equipment at their disposal.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: And how many of these armoured vehicles were forwarded on to the Vukovar front after they were taken from the Varazdin barracks?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot tell you exactly what number, but a number was sent to the Vukovar front, meaning the line of separation between the Croatian army and the JNA, and it does not mean the area of -- the city of Vukovar itself, because we did not have such equipment or type of weapons within the city of Vukovar itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: General, are you familiar with the crimes that occurred in some of the barracks after the blockade was lifted and the ZNG attacked some of the barracks, such as the one in Bjelovar?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that when some of the barracks were taken, there was resistance by the JNA. I also know that when the Bjelovar barracks was taken, there was a powerful explosion in the warehouse, killing a major and some privates or non-commissioned officers. A number of people were killed. I know that when the barracks was taken, some individuals who defended the barracks were also killed. I don't know how many, and I'm not sure we can call it a crime. That's a different issue. They opened fire on Bjelovar, causing damage to a number of buildings and killing civilians, and that was days before the barracks was taken.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Could we perhaps call it a crime we know that the barracks commander was killed, once the ZNG had taken the barracks? Is this something you're familiar with?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Once the barracks was taken, I know that the commander was a colonel named Kovacic, if I remember correctly, and he was killed. How he was killed, whether it was while the barracks were still in the process of being taken or whether it was afterwards is not something that I can say.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Were there other casualties like this one in other barracks in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know about the Gospic barracks. When it was taken, a high-ranking JNA officer was captured. Others were probably captured too, but there was this one Macedonian, I believe, a high-ranking JNA officer. I can't remember his name. Some other barracks that were taken -- I can't remember right now anything specific about any casualties. I know that when the one in Delnice was taken, two days later planes bombed the warehouse there and a lot of the weapons and ammunition were destroyed. Some civilians who were nearby were killed too, but I'm not familiar with any details.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Were there casualties when the ZNG entered the Samobor barracks?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't say. I do know that on that occasion -- well, one reason I remember Samobor is because it was then that we found a document containing a JNA directive for action in Croatia. That's the one reason I remember Samobor. That's why I mentioned it. As for casualties, there were probably casualties on both sides, but it's hard for me now to specify.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Do you know that during the war there was a camp at the Zagreb fair, the grounds of the Zagreb fair, where people of Serb ethnicity were being held?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't know about it at the time, but I know that things were being said in the media after the war, that there were individuals who had their own private warehouses where they kept weapons and ammunition and where they even kept certain people detained. Who those people were is not something that I can say, but it was part of the Pakracka Poljana case, which was a much-discussed trial -- case in Croatia, but I can't specify who the people were on either of these sides.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: And who were the people who had those private warehouses who were keeping those other people there? Is this perhaps something that you can tell us a little about?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think those people belonged to the Croatian Defence Ministry because they dealt with our logistics, obtaining weapons, storing weapons and equipment. If those were indeed warehouses or storage areas, then those people must have been members of the defence ministry.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Do you know anything about the activities of armed units set up by the Croatian Party of Right, Mr. Paraga more specifically?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Paraga and the Croatian Party of Right set up a unit known as H-O-S, HOS, sometime in mid-October. Croatia's liberation forces. I know that in some areas there were incidents involving disobedience, or insubordination to use the mildest possible term, by some of the members of that unit as well as some other units. News of this spread quickly through Croatia. Order had to be re-established, which it was by order of the president, the Supreme Commander. Those units were disbanded. There were no longer any HOS units. They were integrated into the Croatian army and they had to abide by all the rules of discipline that applied. So they existed for a brief while, but I do know that at one point in time they did exist as a separate unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Were they neo-Nazi? Were they not in fact a continuation of the Ustasha tradition?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sure there were people who saw themselves that way, who thought it was their mission to do that. However, the general orientation of the young men I knew who were HOS members was nothing like Ustasha and nothing like neo-Nazi. I'm sure there were people like that, though, both in terms of insignia that some people were wearing, both in terms of the songs they sang, both in terms of their salute and other things, but it was certainly not an official policy that was promoted by the Croatian leadership or the Croatian government.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: You said that early in August - I think it was the 10th, you said - you became Chief of Staff of the National Guards Corps. Did you know that on the 1st of August, President Tudjman called on the Croatian population to prepare themselves for an all-out war?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure about that particular call, but there were calls before this time and after, similar ones. I'm not sure if this is the right time or place to say it, but I think it was on or about the 20th of August that I reported to him personally on the situation that prevailed in the ZNG, having been invited by him to share my opinion. I complained about the lack of weapons and ammunition, especially as the war was ablaze throughout Croatia. And he said, "Don't be in a hurry, don't worry about ammunition, don't worry about weapons. There will be no war." I was simply stunned by this because I realised what the situation was. Areas, certain areas, were sealed off, which amounted to more than 30 per cent, perhaps more, of the Croatian territory, and he said there won't be a war, we'll reach an agreement. And yet there was war already and everybody could see that. So he did call on the Croatian people, probably then, maybe later, but in a private conversation he told me what I'm telling you now. He said that I shouldn't press ahead with weapons or ammunition.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Given your position at the time, could you understand where he got the conclusion from? Was it based on talks that he had had with President Milosevic or something else?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is what I believed to be the provenance of this position. Another source might have been his contacts with the international community, who assured him that they would place pressure on the JNA to not start a war.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Can we agree that early in December, rather on the 1st of December, 1991 Croatia had its own representatives in the federal organs or bodies of the SFRY, that at the time Stjepan Mesic was president of the SFRY Presidency, that the SFRY prime minister was another Croat, Ante Markovic that the foreign minister was Budimir Loncar, that the federal secretary for All People's Defence was another person of Croatian origin, Veljko Kadijevic, with the former three gentlemen being Croatian nationalists. Can we agree on that?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can you just repeat the date for me, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Up until early December 1991. That's what I'm talking about. Let me remind you, it was on the 5th of December, 1991 that Stjepan Mesic stated in front of the parliament, "I have completed my task. There is no more Yugoslavia."

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that assertion is correct. But your assertion that up until early December, those persons held the highest posts or positions in those federal bodies, well, I can't say that it's entirely inaccurate, because formally speaking, perhaps they were still there whether people were filling out forms and one of the forms said, president of the Presidency, and then next to that was the name of Stjepan Mesic. But I know for a fact that this president of the Presidency, as you call him, sometime in October or November, I'm sure there is a record of this somewhere, namely that he wrote an order to the federal secretary for All People's Defence for all units to withdraw to their barracks. Not a letter of that order was complied with, if we consider the problem, the situation with the barracks. So what does it mean, formally speaking somebody is the president but the most important element, the army, is disobeying him? Secondly, if I may, the prime minister, as of the 7th of October, 1991 can no longer go to Belgrade. There was an assassination attempt in Serbia. So what sort of leaders are these? What sort of presidents, if the army, the JNA, is clearly trying to kill them?

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: General, what would you say if I told you that Mr. Herbert Okun, who was adviser to the personal envoy of the UN Secretary-General, stated that on the 18th of November he met Mr. Ante Markovic in Belgrade. Therefore, there seemed to be no danger? Quite the contrary, in fact. He seems to have been meeting high representatives from all over the world and Europe at the time.

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The last time I saw Mr. Ante Markovic was on the 7th of October, 1991 after he left Banski Dvori, the presidential palace in Zagreb, which had just been targeted by the JNA air force. In the building at the time were president of the Presidency, Stjepan Mesic, Prime Minister Ante Markovic and president of the Republic of Croatia, Franjo Tudjman. I know that after that he left for Graz. I'm not sure if he returned to Belgrade. I can't say. But I am fully convinced that he had no role to play any longer, no matter where his office was. Might as well have been in Washington. Neither of these two had any role to play.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: You agree, however, that if he'd had no role to play, I don't think Mr. Cyrus Vance would have seen him and talked to him in trying to reach a solution to the Yugoslav crisis?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think his only role was in trying to reach some sort of a solution for the Yugoslav crisis. But the only influence he had was on the Croatian side. The Slovenes were long gone but he was still influential with the Croatian side. He hails from Croatia and he talked to them. As for the Yugoslav side, the Serb side, his influence was zero. It's as simple as that. It's as if he had no longer held that post at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Be that as it may, we agree that until December, Croatia had not formally withdrawn their representatives from the federal bodies. They were still, formally speaking, there on Croatia's behalf?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think that's true strictly speaking, but I can't guarantee that, not being in expert in that area. What I'm saying is that on the 8th of October, 1991 Croatia adopted a decision to disregard federal laws, regulations, and the constitution as far as secession from the SFRY was concerned. So if it was still sending representatives to Belgrade, well, then, they were lying to themselves, which I don't believe was the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: Your Honours? If I may interrupt my learned friend and object, if I may, to this line of questioning which seems to be very political in nature and calls for a great deal of speculation on the part of the witness and that perhaps the questions could be more focused on military matters, which the witness is in a better position to deal. I haven't mentioned this before, but it does seem that my learned friend is going very broadly into areas of which the witness does not have particular expertise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: There was one question in which that became an issue. Until then, I think the questioning generally has been directed at military matters, though unquestionably with a political flavour. I would not think there is any basis at the moment for disturbing Mr. Vasic's cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. Just a minute, please. There is a problem with my headset. It's fine now, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I think I was the problem, Mr. Vasic. My -- there are ear phones near my microphone and I'm causing a feedback.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, that's taken care of now, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: You talked about negotiations with the JNA today. In your testimony before this Tribunal, did you mention that during the combat operations, you kept a personal diary?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I wrote down as much as I managed to jot down but not everything. However, it would be very useful to me now.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Do you still have that diary?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Did my learned friends from the Prosecution ask to look at that diary in order to check your assertions and to refresh your memory?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They didn't specifically ask for my diary or for copies of excerpts from the diary. I did, however, give them some documents that I had from the negotiations phase with the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Can you please tell us the period during which you kept your diary?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I kept the diary from the time I became the chief of the Main Staff of the ZNG. I do, however, also have a lot of notes or entries from 1986 onwards.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Are you still keeping a diary?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Not anymore. Retired persons don't really keep diaries. However, when I was active at all my posts, I jotted down as much as I could. Unfortunately, I did not jot down everything. I'm saying that again.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: You told my learned friend from the Prosecution today in response to a question about the signing of the agreement on the 21st of October on the change of the convoy route and that agreement was signed on the basis of a prior oral agreement. Can you please tell us, under whose orders did the ZNG members fire at the column of vehicles which was going in the direction of Nustar on the 21st? Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: IMRA AGOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I don't know. But I know that Nustar's defence held up throughout the whole period of the war. They did very well. I don't know what they felt at the moment when the convoy passed by and came to that side. I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, General.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have no further questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Vasic. Mr. Borovic, the time would suggest you could have seven minutes. Do you think you would be more efficiently organised if we started at 2.15 tomorrow or would you like the seven minutes now?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. I think that it would be better to start tomorrow, and I'm not going to need so much time tomorrow. So these seven minutes now might not be the best possible option that I'm being offered. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Very well. We will adjourn now and we will resume at 2.15 tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: be reconvened on Tuesday, the 22nd day of November, 2005, at 2.15 p.m.
